english.html: marriage would never have been worth anything. Natural impotence may also come from being castrated by nature, or born without testicles (I prefer here to flay the Latin [eschorcher le Latin: to force the Latin word into French] rather than to express this word more clearly in unseemly words), or else from having the conduit and passage of the seed naturally so twisted that the seed, constrained to halt in this detour, cannot follow, run down, nor be carried to the necessary places. q This impotence of nature may also be proper and particular to the woman, when she should lack the natural instrument, or be in her secret parts so tight and narrow, or otherwise hindered, that she could not suffer the carnal company of a man r; in which case, if there is no remedy to open the passage, it is certain that the marriage contracted could be dissolved ſ, or, to speak better, declared to have been in no wise and invalidly contracted t. Accidental impotence is either forced and violent, or secret and hidden. Forced impotence comes from the sword and the knife, when by it the member of the man is found cut off u; and although some also do it voluntarily, nevertheless nature remains forced x. Whereupon some allege, rather ill to the purpose as it seems to me, Saint Matthew, when he says that there are some eunuchs who are so born from their mothers' womb, and others who have been made eunuchs by men, and some who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven y. For the Evangelist (whose design is other than the aim of our discourse) means that those who are eunuchs by nature, or by the force of men, if they are chaste and continent, ought not to carry off great praise for it, inasmuch as their chastity proceeds more from constraint and necessity than from honest affection and Christian virtue; but those who have made themselves eunuchs, not by sword or knife (for that is a detestable and accursed thing), but for the honour of God, reverence for His Gospel, and ardent desire to obey His commandments, render themselves victorious over the ardour and concupiscence of the flesh, quenching the fire and the flame which continually burns the flesh: these certainly

notes.gloss: It evidently belongs to the opening clause of p042, "such a marriage would never have been worth anything", or to the castrated by nature that follows; cited again at {t} as "§ Si vero cited above".

uncertain.note: page quality: this is the CUDL colour scan and it is clean and sharp — far better than the p041 microfilm. Ink is even, the paper unstained, no damage, no manuscript marks. Almost every reading below is a fine-detail judgement, not a legibility problem. Layout: one running paragraph of 40 lines filling the whole column, no heading, no foot citation block, no signature, no catchword, no ornament. Body lines 1-40 continue the sentence begun on p041 and run on to p043.

the marginal note keyed p has NO marker anywhere in the body of this page. Lines 1-8 were checked letter by letter at 3-7x; the only wide gap (between 'rien' and 'valu' on line 1) is clean justification space with no ink at all. p041's last marker is {o}, so p is the expected next letter and the note is printed beside body line 1; either the sort was omitted or it belongs to p041's final line. Recorded as a note with key p and no marker, per conventions §4.

uncertain.text: relle peut prouenir auſsi d'eſtre chaſtré de nature, ou
uncertain.note: 'auſsi' here is long s + ROUND s, verified at 3x: the second letter is a short round s with no ascender. The same word is set with the ſſ ligature on lines[8] ('auſſi propre') and lines[20] ('aucuns auſſi'). The difference is deliberate compositor's practice, not a reading error; all three were checked separately.

uncertain.text: le membre de l'homme ſe rrouue coupé {u}. & bien que
uncertain.note: sic: 'ſe rrouue' for 'ſe trouue' (wrong sort r for t, clear at 4x). The marker is an italic u, confirmed against the key letter of margin note u and distinct from the italic x of lines[21]; the sequence t, u, x agrees. The point after {u} is very lightly inked, a small baseline dot before '&', read as a period.

uncertain.text: ture demeure forcee {x}. Sur quoy quelques vns alleguẽt
uncertain.note: two pale brown horizontal marks sit over the 'u' of 'Sur' and over the 'uo' of 'quoy'. At 9x they are much lighter and thinner than the printed tildes on this page ('naturellemẽt', 'alleguẽt', 'cõtrainte') and are read as show-through/foxing, not tildes: 'Sũr' and 'quõy' are not words. Reader B may transcribe tildes here.

uncertain.text: neceſſité, que d'honneſte affection & vertu Chreſtiẽne.
uncertain.note: the mark over the second e of 'Chreſtiẽne' is a horizontal wavy bar (tilde), not the steeply slanted acute this font uses on 'chaſtré', 'né', 'entortilé'. Read as a tilde = 'Chreſtienne'. Reader B may read 'Chreſtiéne'.

three line breaks are printed with no word-break hyphen and are transcribed as printed: lines[5] 'contrain' + lines[6] 'te'; lines[13] 'cõtracté' is a whole word but lines[13]/lines[14] run on without one; margin note q likewise breaks 'par'/'tium.' unhyphenated. Hyphens are printed normally elsewhere on the page ('natu-', 'ſe-', 'char-', 'L'im-', 'violen-', 'na-', 'comman-', 'concupi-'), so these are compositor omissions.

spacing: the compositor repeatedly sets punctuation tight ('valu.L'impuiſſance', 'que,exprimer', 'honneſtes)ou', 'neceſſaires.q', 'eſtroitte,ou', 'paſſage,il', '&inualablemẽt') and sometimes with a space before ('nature , ou', 'cachee . L'impuiſſance', 'meres : &'), and sets 'ſemẽcecontrain' and 'la ſe-' solid. All normalized to single spaces per §1; no letter is added or removed.
set in spaced capitals and closed up here per §3. No terminal punctuation is printed after DV. The folio '42' stands at the left of the same line and matches the manifest.
the break sign after 'nou' is a raised mid-height dot rather than a stroke; transcribed as the word-break hyphen ('nou-|uelles') per §1. The same citation at p041 note b prints 'nou' with no sign.

the numeral is three minims carrying three dots, the last descending: read 'iij'. The same citation at p041 note b reads 'col iiij.' (four), so the two pages disagree; 'iiij' cannot be wholly excluded, but only three dots and three strokes are visible at 10x.

printed solid as 'Gal.auxv.' There is a hair more space between 'u' and 'x' than between 'a' and 'u', and the sense requires 'au xv. li. de vſu. partium' (Galen, De usu partium, book XV), as the conventions' own example prints 'au xv. liur. de'. Split as 'au xv.' per the §1 word-division rule; 'aux v.' is the alternative reading.

the vowel after 'qu' is a single italic 'a' with no 'e' joined to it, so 'quaritur' is transcribed as printed; the Digest lemma is 'l. quaeritur', so an æ ligature (or a missing e) is what the compositor meant. Not modernized.

the small mark after 'tatis' has a tail below the baseline at 10x and is read as a comma; a point with a flaw cannot be wholly excluded. The parallel citation on p041 (note l) has 'de frig. & malef.' after a point.

the final point after 'vij' is very faint and small; included on the parallel of the other citation endings in this note. The numeral 'vij' carries two dots and a descending j, the same form as 'iij' at the start of the line.

the print sets 'l.lege .P. fi'; the pale mark between 'lege' and 'P' read as a lightly inked point (both readers). The last letter pair is 'fi' (italic f with a crossbar through the stem), continued by 'nal.' on the next line: '§ finali'. Both readers read 'ſi'.
first word read 'nal' (italic n, a, l) completing 'fi|nal'; reader A read 'mal', reader B 'ual'. The faint baseline point after it is kept. 'D. de ſic-|car.' = ad legem Corneliam de sicariis.
no point is printed after the initial 'l'; checked at 10x, the gap between 'l' and 'ſi' is empty. Compare note r lines[0] 'l. quaritur.' and note x lines[0] 'l. lege', which both carry one.

It is not a normalized long s. Contrast blocks[0].lines[37] 'victorieux ſur l'ardeur', where the lowercase word is correctly set with ſ.

readings.reason: At 4x the letter after 'ſe' is a plain r (stem with a shoulder flag, no crossbar, no curled foot), identical to the r that follows it; wrong sort for 'trouue', transcribed as printed (sic). The marker at the end of the line is an italic u (two-stroke, open top), not an x, and a faint baseline dot follows it before '&'.

At 5x the mark after 'nou' is a small round dot set at mid x-height, level with the letters' middles, whereas the point after 'ro' on the same line sits on the baseline. A raised mid-dot at the line end where the word continues ('nou|uelles') is this print's word-break sign; transcribed '-' per §1.

At 10x a mark is printed after 'tatis' (B omitted it): a compact dot with a short tail curling down and left below the baseline, unlike the round baseline point after 'frig.' on the same line. Read as a comma.

At 8x the first letter has two arches joined at the top and is open at the foot (italic n, two strokes, not the three of an m and not the open-topped u); the word continues the previous line's 'fi' (see margin_notes[6].lines[0]) to give '§ fi|nal.' = § finali, which resolves the citation (l. Lege Cornelia, § fin., D. de sicariis). A faint baseline point follows 'nal', kept.

Shared reading corrected: at 8x the letter after 'P.' carries a crossbar that runs through the stem into the i (italic f), not the left-only nub of the italic ſ of 'ſic-' below; the word is 'fi|nal' (§ finali), per §2 decide ſ/f by the word.
